sources.citation: Jepson, Kathleen. 2025. Contrastive vowel length and segment duration in production and perception in Djambarrpuyŋu. Laboratory Phonology 16(1). doi:10.16995/labphon.10161 (open access, 49 pp).
sources.quote: 'In Djambarrpuyŋu, the vowel length contrast is restricted to the first syllable of the word, a position which is also the putative location of fixed word stress (Wilkinson, 2012).' Sec. 2.3: 'Morphy (1983) reports for Djapu that in disyllabic words where the first/stressed syllable is open, the duration of the following consonant varies according to the length of the stressed vowel ...' — treats Morphy as the Djapu source; no different stress position proposed.
sources.locator: sec. 1 Introduction (p. 2); sec. 2.3 (pp. 7-8) summarising Morphy 1983 p.25 on Djapu
sources.note: Open-access instrumental paper that restates initial fixed stress for Djambarrpuyŋu and summarises Morphy 1983's Djapu stress/gemination analysis; corroborating secondary citation.

sources.citation: Jepson, Kathleen. 2019. Prosody, prominence and segments in Djambarrpuyŋu. PhD thesis, University of Melbourne (hdl 11343/227802), 364 pp.
sources.quote: Abstract: 'Word stress patterns previously reported for Djambarrpuyŋu include primary stress on the initial syllable and second stresses assigned to alternating odd syllables ... The results of a quantitative acoustic analysis partially support the previous description. The initial syllable of words does have the highest fundamental frequency of all syllables within a word. However, other correlates of prominence ... are not found ... evidence for secondary stress ... is not found'. p.14: 'Wilkinson (2012, p. 62) states that "[s]tress patterning in Djambarrpuyŋu is largely predictable", with t
sources.locator: Abstract p. iv; sec. 1.2.2.5 'Previous treatment of stress' p. 14; ch. 5 'Word stress in Djambarrpuyŋu' pp. 140ff
sources.note: Only instrumental study of word stress in a Dhuwal variety (sister dialect of Djapu); confirms initial primary stress by f0 and finds no evidence for secondary stress — supports coding primary-only initial stress.

sources.citation: Wood, Ray. 1978. Some Yuulngu phonological patterns. In Papers in Australian Linguistics No. 11, Pacific Linguistics A-51: 53-117. Canberra: ANU. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/144561).
sources.quote: For Gälpu (Galiwin'ku; Dhangu group, a different Yolngu languoid): 'Stress patterning is predictable, and is regulated by three factors: (a) All words contain stress groups consisting of two or three syllables, of which only the initial syllable carries stress; (b) Morpheme boundaries between roots of reduplicated and compound stems affect the patterning; (c) The initial syllable of a word carries primary stress.' 3.6 Exceptions: 'mainly pronominals' plus a few words with second-syllable stress (pu'ralku 'placename', pur'wu 'flower', pa'ngak 'still').
sources.note: Earliest explicit Yolngu stress analysis (Gälpu): initial primary stress, 2-3 syllable stress groups, listed lexical exceptions; the model Wilkinson follows for Dhuwal secondary stress. Related variety only.
sources.venue: Papers in Australian Linguistics No. 11, Pacific Linguistics A-51: 53-117

sources.citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 1980. Dhuwal (Arnhem Land) texts on kinship and other subjects, with grammatical sketch and dictionary. Oceania Linguistic Monographs 23. Sydney. iv+241 pp. (MPG PuRe item_2049456, public PDF).
sources.quote: Sketch is 'biased towards the Jambarpuyngu (Jam) dialect, although Jap [Djapu] data are presented when available'. Phonology chapter gives no word-stress rule; only 'Long vowels occur only in word-initial syllables' and incidental remarks (nga:thil 'a regular word with full word-stress on the long vowel').
